Title: 6. Let Bulls Smell Flowers, Not Blood: A Call to Ban Bullfighting
Text:
Co-submitted by: Radikal Ungdom, Svensk Ungdom, LUF, Joventut Nacionalista de Catalunya

Co-signed by: Keskustanuoret, Centerpartiets Ungdomsförbund, Unge Venstre, Young Green Liberals, JOVD, Mladé Progresívne Slovensko, Jongliberalen, Jonge Demokraten, Lithuanian Liberal Youth, Jeunes MR

Recognising that:

  • Bullfighting has existed as a cultural tradition in several European countries, including Spain, Portugal, and southern France, for centuries
  • Traditions rooted in economic and cultural practice have already been overridden by the European Union on animal-welfare grounds.
  • The European Union has previously exempted bullfighting from animal welfare legislation under the cultural heritage clause, allowing member states to maintain the practice.
  • Council Regulation (EC) 1099/2009 on the protection of animals at the time of killing excludes animals killed during cultural or sporting events from its scope, meaning bulls killed in the ring are not subject to the welfare standards applied to animals slaughtered for food. 
  • Bullfighting is a contest involving a human voluntarily immobilising, injuring and/or killing a bull. This should not be confused with other contests involving other animals, such as Swiss cow fighting, which do not involve direct human intervention and are not detrimental to animal welfare.

Noting that:

  • Bullfighting causes severe and deliberate physical and psychological suffering to bulls, in direct contradiction with the principle of animal sentience recognised in Article 13 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU).
  • Bullfighting also carries serious risks to human life: recorded data show that 134 people have been killed by bulls in Spain over the past century, with many more suffering serious injuries. These events require publicly funded emergency and security services, reinforcing the industry's public subsidy.
  • Public support for bullfighting is in sharp decline across Europe, including in Spain, where a majority of the population, and particularly young people, oppose the practice.
  • The framing of bullfighting as "cultural heritage" sets a dangerous precedent by allowing cultural tradition to override fundamental ethical and animal welfare standards.
  • There are regions, such as Catalonia and the Canary Islands, where bullfighting is already mostly abolished.
  • Bull-breeding farms continue to receive Common Agricultural Policy direct payments regardless of whether the animals are destined for the bullring, meaning EU taxpayers indirectly subsidise the practice.
  • Spanish regulation (Real Decreto 1086/2020) classifies the killing of bulls in bullfights as "emergency slaughter" under Regulation (EC) 853/2004, a classification that raises food safety concerns where such meat enters the human food chain.

Believing that:

  • The deliberate killing and torture of animals for entertainment is fundamentally incompatible with a humane society, regardless of cultural or historical tradition.
  • No tradition should be permitted to override the Union's commitment to animal sentience and welfare.
  • In Spain, France and Portugal, 77% of the population considers bullfighting to cause unacceptable animal suffering, and 58% want it banned, numbers that are difficult to reconcile with continued public support for the tradition.
  • A just transition must be offered to workers and breeders currently dependent on the bullfighting industry, to ensure that ending the practice does not come at the expense of rural livelihoods.

LYMEC calls for:

  • All member states to ban bullfighting, and calls on the Commission to support and coordinate such efforts. 
  • The revision of Article 13 TFEU to remove or narrow the cultural exemption insofar as it permits practices causing deliberate and severe animal suffering
  • The European Commission to revise Regulation (EC) 1099/2009 to remove the exemption for cultural and sporting events, ensuring bulls killed in bullfights are subject to the same welfare protections as other slaughtered animals
  • An immediate end to all direct and indirect public subsidies at local, regional, and national level, directed towards the breeding, training, or staging of bullfighting.
  • The European Commission to investigate the classification of bullring killings as "emergency slaughter" under Regulation (EC) 853/2004, given its implications for food safety.
  • The Commission and Member States to establish transition support schemes for workers and breeders affected by the phase-out of the bullfighting industry. The reallocation of Common Agricultural Policy funds currently supporting bull-breeding towards the conservation of rural ecosystems, ensuring that the animals currently bred for the bullring can be maintained in natural sanctuaries rather than being subjected to deliberate suffering.
Category: Chatper 3 - Culture, Education, Youth, Science and Technology

Title: 7. Together We Spend, United We Ball - More EU Defense Joint Venture Projects!
Text:
Submitted by: Nowoczesna Youth (Poland)

Co-signed by: Mladé Progresívne Slovensko (Slovakia), Young Green Liberals (Switzerland), Gibanje Svoboda Mladi (Slovenia), Joventut Nacionalista de Catalunya, USR Tineret (Romania), ZeMolodizhka (Ukraine), PSG Mladi (Serbia), Junge Liberale (Germany), Liberal Democratic League of Ukraine (Ukraine), Lithuanian Liberal Youth (Lithuania), 

Considering that:

  • The escalation of the Russian aggression poses a threat to all of Europe.
  • Reducing external dependencies within the EU strengthens its military position and strategic autonomy.
  • Pooling demand gives EU countries greater market leverage when negotiating with major defense contractors.
  • The fragmentation of European defence procurement and industrial capabilities leads to unnecessary duplication, higher costs, and limited economies of scale across the EU.
  • The European Defence Technological and Industrial Base remains unevenly distributed among Member States, making cross-border cooperation and the inclusion of small and medium-sized enterprises essential for strengthening Europe’s defence resilience and supply chains.
  • Major European collaborative programmes such as the A400M and Eurofighter have strengthened Europe’s technological and industrial capabilities and created cross-border industrial cooperation, while also experiencing significant delays and cost overruns linked in part to differing national requirements and complex multinational programme management.
  • The interoperability of European armed forces is hindered by differences in technical standards, military requirements and procurement procedures, limiting the effectiveness of joint European defence capabilities.


Believing that:

  • In times of crisis, cooperation and unity of European states is key to sustaining peace and prosperity within the region.
  • Liberal democracies must act decisively to deter authoritarian regimes from violating territorial integrity and international law, as failing to do so would erode the values that bind Europe together.
  • Joint rearmament programs such as SAFE bring European countries together in an effort to enhance our defence capabilities in order to deter Russia and any other external threats.
  • European countries must be capable of developing European-made defence frameworks instead of depending on foreign aid and foreign military programs. 
  • European defence has to be made in Europe whenever it is possible.
  • Europe should move towards becoming self-sustainable in terms of producing military defence capabilities.
  • Joint rearmament projects enforce the necessity of cooperation between different EU member-states, thus reducing the threat of intra-EU frictions in decades to come.


LYMEC Calls For:

  • The establishment of a functional, coordinated EU Defense Joint Venture framework, operating along the lines of the ReArm Europe Plan, and aimed at the acceleration of joint development and production of the most critical military components by the EU member states.
  • The acceleration (and, wherever it is possible, expansion) of the ongoing EU cross-border defense projects, particularly within the spheres of drone and counter-drone systems, air and missile defense, cyber defense, and long-range precision strike capabilities - expanding on the already-existing frameworks such as the EDPCI and PESCO.
  • Bolstering the European Defense Technological and Industrial Base by promoting new cross-border industrial partnerships, supporting smaller and medium-sized enterprises, encouraging joint European research and development, with a particular focus on dual-use technologies that serve both civilian and military purposes, and ensuring a network of strong, resilient European supply chains.
  • The drive towards a unified, EU-wide approach to defense and industrial cooperation, manifested by the harmonization of technical and procurement standards, military requirements, and common capability priorities, with the goal of achieving interoperability between the EU armed forces and reducing the unnecessary area of overlap between their national defense programmes.
  • The incorporation of a permanent, EU-level mechanism aimed at the monitoring and coordination of the EU defense joint venture projects, as well as ensuring transparency and implementation of deadlines, regularly reporting to the European Parliament.
  • The strengthening of defence industrial cooperation between the EU and Ukraine through joint research, development, production and procurement, particularly in drone and counter-drone technologies, building on Ukraine’s battlefield experience and innovation, while further integrating Ukrainian defence companies into European defence industrial projects and supply chains.

Title: 4. Securing Europe’s Digital Future
Text:
Co-submitted by: JMR, JOVD, JNC

Co-signed by: Svensk Ungdom, VU, Radikal Ungdom, Jonge Democraten, Lithuanian Liberal Youth, Junge liberale NEOS - JUNOS, Jungfreisinnige Schweiz

Considering that:

  • Cybersecurity threats, including increasingly AI-enabled attacks, are growing in sophistication and increasingly affect European democratic institutions, critical infrastructure and the economy, while growing reliance on digital systems makes cyber resilience essential to public safety, fundamental rights and European sovereignty;
  • Fragmented implementation, overlapping reporting requirements and inconsistent supervision can undermine cybersecurity and the European Single Market;
  • European cybersecurity companies face barriers to scaling, while public and private organisations need accessible, trustworthy and affordable security solutions;
  • NIS2 transposition remains deeply uneven across Member States, with significant divergences in the definition of “significant incident”, in notification deadlines and in administrative procedures, creating a fragmented compliance burden for companies operating across multiple markets;
  • Advances in artificial intelligence, autonomous systems and computing can strengthen cyber defence while changing attack capabilities and challenging existing safeguards, including cryptographic protection;
  • Dependence on a single technology provider or jurisdiction can expose essential services to disruption, coercion and supply-chain compromise;

Noting that:

  • European cybersecurity legislation, including NIS2, the Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) and the Cyber Solidarity Act, together with the AI Act, provides a basis for enforceable protection that must evolve with threats;
  • A dedicated EU-wide certification scheme for Managed Security Services (MSS) is being developed under the Cybersecurity Act, but the market is not yet fully covered by the “certify once, sell anywhere” principle;
  • Interoperability, data portability and the ability to switch providers can reduce strategic dependencies and improve resilience;
  • Cooperation through ENISA, national incident response teams and CERT-EU provides a basis for shared exercises, threat information exchange and assistance across borders; and can be extended through working arrangements to trusted European non-EU partners such as Switzerland, whose economies, supply chains and critical infrastructure are closely interconnected with the Single Market.
  • Ensuring proportionate oversight and incident reporting for high-risk AI systems used in cybersecurity and critical services, including appropriate human oversight and safeguards for autonomous systems;
  • The debate over the EU Cloud Services Scheme (EUCS) has been stalled for years by the conflict between sovereignty requirements (EU headquarters, European control) and open-market principles, without a stable balance having yet been found;
  • The transition to post-quantum cryptography constitutes a strategic resilience challenge that current EU cybersecurity policy has not fully addressed, despite the timeline already set by the Commission and the NIS Cooperation Group;
  • European SMEs, particularly cybersecurity startups, report regulatory compliance burden, not lack of market opportunity, as their primary practical obstacle;
  • The European Union is exploring light mutual-recognition arrangements on cybersecurity certification with trusted non-EU partners, including Japan, Singapore, Canada and the United Kingdom, allowing EU-certified products and services to gain streamlined access to their markets;
  • The application of the first reporting obligations under the CRA from September 2026 marks a turning point for product security, but risks adding a dual layer of incident reporting alongside NIS2 for hardware and software manufacturers;


Believing that:

  • Cybersecurity is a shared responsibility, requiring clear and proportionate duties for public authorities, technology providers and operators;
  • Security requirements should reflect the likelihood and severity of harm and the criticality of services, with practical support for smaller organisations and public oversight proportionate to risk;
  • Technology-neutral rules should protect innovation, competition and legitimate research, while requiring evidence of adequate safeguards for serious risks; building European capabilities should reduce strategic dependencies while preserving secure international cooperation;
  • Strategic autonomy requires skills, secure infrastructure and viable alternatives, alongside cooperation with democratic partners and evidence-based assessment of foreign interference risks;
  • Europe’s growing reliance on AI makes the ability to independently develop, evaluate and operate capable AI models and their supporting infrastructure essential to cybersecurity and strategic autonomy;
  • dependence on providers subject to foreign jurisdiction can expose European research, businesses and public services to supply disruption, external political pressure and loss of control over sensitive data;
  • European AI sovereignty should therefore rest on competitive domestic capabilities, diversified supply chains and secure cooperation with democratic partners, rather than technological isolation or protectionism;
  • European strategic autonomy in encryption and critical infrastructure must rest on clear, funded technical timelines, not only on general principles of dependency reduction;
  • Cybersecurity must uphold privacy, strong encryption, due process and democratic accountability; technical standards must remain adaptable without weakening these principles;
  • Mutual recognition of cybersecurity certification with trusted non-EU partners should be pursued as a complement to, not a substitute for, a strong and harmonised internal European framework;

LYMEC calls for:

1. Strengthening the European cybersecurity workforce by:

  • Promoting common European cybersecurity skills frameworks and qualifications, while recognising practical experience and diverse entry routes;
  • Expanding partnerships between education providers, public authorities and businesses for apprenticeships, traineeships and lifelong learning, including recruitment pathways for local government and underrepresented groups;
  • Embedding practical digital security education in schools and regular workforce training, including for decision-makers, adapted to evolving fraud, social engineering and incident-response needs;
  • Providing accessible funding and technical assistance to SMEs and municipalities for cybersecurity assessments, remediation and shared expertise;
  • Supporting the CSC-EDIC in implementing the ECSF and encouraging broader Member State participation;

2. Strengthening the European cybersecurity Single Market by:

  • Calling on EU institutions and Member States to ensure coherent implementation, effective supervision and interoperable incident reporting, while regularly reviewing requirements to keep them proportionate and effective;
  • Promoting interoperable standards and proportionate certification and procurement requirements, ensuring that certification is carried out by independent conformity assessment bodies accredited by national accreditation bodies and supervised by national cybersecurity certification authorities under the Cybersecurity Act, and that valid certificates, including ISO/IEC 27001 certificates covering the relevant requirements, are recognised across Member States, while avoiding duplicate certification;
  • Harmonising the definition of “significant incident” and reporting timelines across Member States as a priority within the ongoing NIS2 review, to reduce the fragmented compliance landscape currently faced by cross-border entities;
  • Ensuring that manufacturers placing digital products on the EU market provide security by design and default, clearly disclose the applicable security support period before purchase and provide necessary security fixes during that period without separate charges, consistently with the Cyber Resilience Act;
  • Promoting clear end-of-support notices and practical migration guidance so that users can make informed choices about replacing unsupported products;
  • Establishing clear legal safeguards for good-faith security researchers who minimise harm, protect personal data and follow coordinated vulnerability disclosure procedures;
  • Accelerating the finalisation of EUCS through a risk-based approach that balances security, strategic autonomy and competition;
  • Completing an EU-wide MSS certification scheme that enables cybersecurity service providers, including SMEs, to benefit from the “certify once, sell anywhere” principle;
  • Addressing AI-related cybersecurity risks through existing regulatory frameworks, with any additional independent testing limited to clearly defined capabilities or uses presenting demonstrable risks of serious harm; recognising equivalent assessments, protecting confidential information and personal data in accordance with Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR), and avoiding duplicate approval procedures;
  • Requiring operators deploying autonomous systems in critical services to limit access to necessary functions, maintain appropriate activity records and test human intervention and service recovery arrangements, proportionate to the consequences of failure; integrating serious-incident reporting into existing notification channels;
  • Ensuring that any authority-imposed remediation requirement or deployment restriction addresses a documented risk, is no broader or longer than necessary, and is subject to reasoned decisions, periodic review and effective appeal;
  • Reducing compliance burden for SMEs and startups through simplified reporting templates, a genuine one-stop shop for incident notification, and proportionate documentation requirements, in line with the Commission’s Digital Omnibus simplification package, proposed in late 2025 and currently under legislative debate;

3. Strengthening European strategic resilience without protectionism by:

  • Calling on Member States and EU institutions to secure public services, including municipal services, through funded, risk-based requirements covering access control, updates, protected backups and tested continuity plans; requiring independent audits at risk-appropriate intervals, assigned remediation deadlines and supervisory follow-up, while testing essential service provision during digital outages;
  • Exploring a common European model agreement on ‘data embassies’, meaning the hosting of backup copies of critical government data and essential public-service systems of one Member State on the territory of another under a treaty-based regime of inviolability and immunity, which would: cover government data only and define the permitted purpose of the facility; exclude remote access by the host State without consent; keep the facility under the sending State’s control rather than a provider subject to third-country jurisdiction; apply recognised security and data-centre standards; provide for a joint committee, dispute resolution and orderly termination; and comply with the GDPR and NIS2.
  • Strengthening cooperation between national incident response teams, ENISA and CERT-EU, including mutual assistance and exercises involving municipalities and essential-service providers; drawing on the expertise of the NATO Cooperative Cyber Defense Centre of Excellence (CCDCOE) in Tallinn, including tis Locked Shields exercise and the Tallinn Manual on international law applicable to cyber operations.
  • Strengthening and adequately funding the EU Cybersecurity Reserve beyond its current scope and budget, so it can respond to a broader range of incidents and support Member States with limited national capacity;
  • Calling on public administrations and critical infrastructure operators to inventory vulnerable cryptographic systems, prioritise data requiring long-term confidentiality, and establish phased migration plans with identified responsibilities, costs and supplier requirements, aligned with the European post-quantum roadmap;
  • Supporting implementation through shared technical guidance, interoperability testing and pooled procurement; using existing funding programmes for targeted, time-limited assistance where SMEs and public administrations demonstrate capacity gaps, with progress measured against defined migration milestones;
  • Requiring critical infrastructure operators to manage supplier concentration and supply-chain risks and maintain viable continuity and exit arrangements;
  • Supporting European cybersecurity startups, SMEs and open-source security projects through access to research, finance and procurement;
  • Exploring links between European cybersecurity industrial policy and the emerging European Defence Single Market to facilitate appropriate access to dual-use funding and cooperation;
  • Deepening cooperation with democratic partners through joint cyber exercises, operational exchanges between incident response teams and cooperation on interoperable security standards;
  • Opposing mandated encryption backdoors that weaken end-to-end encryption and indiscriminate scanning of private communications, while supporting targeted, judicially authorised and proportionate investigative measures consistent with Articles 7 and 8 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union;
  • Limiting threat information sharing to necessary, proportionate purposes, with data minimisation, retention limits and oversight by existing competent authorities;
  • Pursuing mutual-recognition arrangements on cybersecurity certification with
  • trusted non-EU partners such as Japan, Singapore, Canada, Ukraine, Switzerland and the United Kingdom, to open new export opportunities for European cybersecurity companies without compromising EU security and data protections standards;
  • without compromising EU security standards;

Strengthening Europe’s capacity to independently develop, evaluate and operate capable AI models and secure computing infrastructure, reducing strategic dependencies on providers subject to US or Chinese jurisdiction, by:

  • expanding affordable access to high-performance computing, secure cloud infrastructure and competitive research funding for European universities, public research institutions, startups and SMEs;
  • supporting European AI research and development, including open-source models and tools, through transparent, competitive funding focused on research, shared infrastructure and demonstrable capability gaps;
  • ensuring that public procurement promotes interoperability, data portability and the practical ability to switch providers or operate models independently, with safeguards proportionate to the sensitivity and criticality of their use;
  • diversifying critical hardware and infrastructure supply chains while preserving competition and scientific cooperation with trusted democratic partners.
  • without compromising EU security standards;

Strengthening Europe’s capacity to independently develop, evaluate and operate capable AI models and secure computing infrastructure, reducing strategic dependencies on providers subject to US or Chinese jurisdiction, by:

  • securing access to sufficient high-performance computing, secure cloud infrastructure and competitive research funding for European universities, public research institutions, startups and SMEs;
  • supporting European AI research and development, including open-source models and tools, through transparent, competitive funding focused on research, shared infrastructure and demonstrable capability gaps;
  • ensuring that public procurement promotes interoperability, data portability and the practical ability to switch providers or operate models independently, with safeguards proportionate to the sensitivity and criticality of their use;
  • diversifying critical hardware and infrastructure supply chains while preserving competition and scientific cooperation with trusted democratic partners.

4. Strengthening European operational crisis preparedness by:

  • Expanding coordinated cross-border cyber crisis exercises building on existing EU exercise frameworks and the EU Cybersecurity Reserve;
  • Supporting Member States with limited national CSIRT capacity through shared resources and mutual assistance mechanisms;
  • Integrating post-quantum cryptography readiness into critical infrastructure resilience assessments;

Title: 9. No Union without values: defending the Rule of Law in the EU
Text:
Submitted by: USR Tineret

Considering that:

  • Article 2 of the Treaty on European Union establishes respect for human dignity, freedom, democracy, equality, the rule of law and human rights as fundamental values on which the European Union is founded;
  • the European Commission assesses the rule of law in Member States through four key areas: the justice system, the anti-corruption framework, media freedom and institutional checks and balances;
  • LYMEC has previously called for liberal and democratic actors throughout Europe to remain vigilant regarding early signs of democratic backsliding, and has affirmed that European institutions have a responsibility to actively defend the values enshrined in the Treaties (Policy Book - 1.35 – “European funds for European values!”);

Remembering that:

  • the Economist Intelligence Unit’s 2024 Democracy Index downgraded Romania from a “flawed democracy” to a “hybrid regime”, following a decline in Romania’s overall democracy score from 6.45 to 5.99, citing deterioration in electoral processes, the functioning of government, public trust and corruption;
  • the European Commission’s 2026 Rule of Law Report continued to identify challenges in Romania concerning, among others, judicial independence, the effectiveness of anti-corruption measures, media independence, and the transparency and predictability of the legislative process;
  • in August 2026, the Romanian Parliament adopted legislation removing Dominic Fritz, the democratically elected Mayor of Timișoara and leader of Romania’s main reformist party USR, from office. This legislation applied a new legal consequence to a pre-existing situation, in breach of the prohibition of retroactive legislation under Romanian constitutional law and the EU principle of legal certainty, but the Romanian Constitutional Court nevertheless upheld the measure;
  • Dominic Fritz was removed from office based on an administrative conflict of interest for which no concrete financial damage was established rather than a criminal conviction or finding of corruption. This conduct dated November 2020, during the first days of his first term as Mayor of Timișoara, when, instructed by municipal officials, he signed a document concerning a pre-existing urban-planning project whose documentation had been prepared before he took office and had already been signed by his predecessor.

Noting that:

  • democratic backsliding rarely occurs through a single institutional change, but can develop through a series of measures which gradually erode checks and balances, judicial independence, political pluralism, institutional accountability and, ultimately, the foundations of liberal democracy;
  • the weakening of democratic safeguards can occur through formally legal procedures when such procedures are used to undermine institutional independence, restrict political competition or reduce the ability of elected representatives and independent institutions to exercise their mandates.

Believing that:

  • the continued recurrence of rule-of-law concerns in Romania and other EU Member States, despite successive monitoring and recommendations by European institutions, demonstrates the limitations of a system that relies primarily on dialogue and recommendations without sufficiently effective enforcement mechanisms;
  • any political use of the justice system, including the removal of political opponents from office, as it has happened in Romania, is unacceptable and must never be tolerated within the EU. Wherever attempted by Member States, such actions must be prevented or appropriately sanctioned;
  • the European Union cannot fully safeguard its democratic foundations when Member States are permitted to progressively abandon the principles of liberal democracy while retaining the benefits and decision-making rights of Union membership;
  • early signs of democratic backsliding must be addressed promptly, before they become systemic;
  • independent courts and constitutional institutions are essential safeguards of democracy only when their independence, transparency and accountability remain protected from political interference;

Local democracy and local self-government are integral parts of European democracy. National oversight and institutional cooperation are essential, but must not be misused through arbitrary interventions or retroactive legislation to undermine the autonomy of democratically elected local authorities.

  • anti-corruption and integrity legislation is essential to liberal democracy, but its credibility depends on transparent, proportionate and politically neutral enforcement.

LYMEC calls for: 

  • European institutions to make full and consistent use of the legal instruments already at their disposal to address democratic backsliding, strengthen the rule of law, and protect fundamental rights across all Member States;
  • EU institutions to develop stronger early-warning mechanisms allowing potential rule-of-law violations to be addressed before they become systemic;
  • Member States to work towards a new European treaty that establishes binding non-regression standards, proportionate enforcement mechanisms subject to judicial review, and permanent rule-of-law safeguards; 
  • the European Commission to establish clear benchmarks and deadlines for addressing persistent rule-of-law deficiencies identified in its annual Rule of Law Reports, and to make greater use of infringement proceedings where national legislation or administrative practice undermine judicial independence, legal certainty, democratic participation or other rights protected by EU law;
  • EU institutions and Member States to include robust and legally enforceable rule-of-law safeguards in future EU accession treaties, allowing for proportionate corrective measures in cases of serious democratic backsliding after accession, based on clear and objective criteria and subject to judicial review;
  • ALDE Party, Renew Europe and LYMEC Member Organisations to continue to address rule-of-law concerns in all Member States, regardless of the political affiliation of the governments concerned.

Title: 1. Powering Europe Freely - A Technology-Neutral, Competitive and Resilient European Electricity System
Text:
Submitted by: Junge liberale NEOS - JUNOS

Co-signed by: Jóvenes de Ciudadanos, Jongliberalen, Joventut Nacionalista Catalunya, Jeunes MR, Jonge Democraten, Venstres Ungdom, Lithuanian Liberal Youth,

Jongerenorganisatie Vrijheid en Democratie, Liberale Hochschulgruppen , Jungfreisinnige Schweiz

Jongerenorganisatie Vrijheid en Democratie, Liberale Hochschulgruppen , Attīstībai Youth

Noting that: 

  • Europe must rapidly decarbonise its economy while maintaining affordable and reliable electricity supplies and safeguarding its industrial competitiveness; 
  • the electrification of transport, heating and industrial processes will increase the importance of a reliable, affordable and low-carbon electricity system, while tax, levy and tariff structures in some EU Member States continue to disadvantage electricity relative to the direct use of fossil fuels; 
  • EU Member States differ considerably in geography, natural resources, existing infrastructure and public preferences and therefore rely on different electricity mixes, while Article 194 TFEU preserves their right to determine their choice between different energy sources; 
  • renewable energy sources such as wind, solar and hydropower are essential to European decarbonisation, while growing shares of variable generation increase the importance of grids, storage, demand response, interconnection and other sources of flexibility; 
  • nuclear energy provides a substantial share of Europe’s low-carbon electricity and is used by several EU Member States for decarbonisation and security of supply, while requiring the highest standards of safety, security, radiation protection, decommissioning and radioactive-waste management; 
  • Europe remains dependent on external suppliers for parts of several critical electricity-sector supply chains, including parts of the nuclear fuel cycle; 
  • a more interconnected European electricity system allows countries to make better use of different generation profiles, reduce the effects of local shortages and surpluses and increase overall security of supply; 
  • the deployment of new generation, storage and flexible demand is increasingly constrained by lengthy permitting procedures, limited grid-connection capacity and inefficiently managed connection queues; 
  • electricity generation and network infrastructure require substantial long-term investment, while fragmented national licensing requirements and regulatory practices can increase costs, duplicate assessments and impede economies of scale within the European Single Market. 

Acknowledging that: 

  • no electricity technology is without costs, risks, environmental impacts or infrastructure requirements, and technology neutrality therefore requires comparable risks, services and externalities to be assessed through transparent, evidence-based and proportionate criteria rather than all technologies being regulated identically; 
  • the costs and benefits of electricity technologies cannot be meaningfully assessed solely through generation costs but must also account for relevant system effects, including balancing, grids, storage, firm capacity, security of supply, decommissioning, waste management and environmental externalities; 
  • public intervention can be justified where markets cannot adequately provide infrastructure, innovation, security of supply or other public goods, but poorly designed subsidies, price controls and other interventions can distort competition and investment; long-term investment therefore requires regulatory frameworks that are predictable and non-retroactive while remaining open to transparent and proportionate future reform; 
  • energy-only markets and functioning price signals should remain the starting point for coordinating investment, production and consumption, while additional capacity mechanisms may be justified where demonstrable adequacy concerns remain after barriers to interconnection, storage, demand response and market participation have been addressed; 
  • scarce grid capacity should be allocated transparently and efficiently rather than being indefinitely occupied by inactive or speculative projects, while flexible or conditional connection agreements can in some cases enable earlier access without immediate full network reinforcement; 
  • the transition away from fossil-fuel electricity generation must be sufficiently rapid to meet Europe’s climate objectives while avoiding new long-term dependencies on infrastructure that risks becoming economically or environmentally unsustainable; 
  • greater European regulatory cooperation and technical standardisation can reduce unnecessary duplication and enable economies of scale without weakening the independence or ultimate responsibility of competent national safety regulators. 

Believing that: 

  • European electricity policy should pursue climate neutrality, security of supply and affordability by judging technologies according to measurable outcomes—including lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions, safety, environmental impacts, system value and economic efficiency—rather than prescribing a politically preferred technological pathway; 
  • Europe should neither politically mandate nuclear energy nor exclude it from a future climate-neutral electricity system; 
  • competition, carbon pricing and functioning markets are generally better suited to discovering cost-effective solutions than permanent technology-specific subsidies or political micromanagement; 
  • electricity prices provide essential signals of scarcity, abundance, congestion and investment needs; affordability concerns and energy poverty should therefore primarily be addressed through targeted support rather than broad price caps or permanent administrative price-setting that suppress these signals; 
  • taxation, network charges and regulation should, as far as possible, reflect measurable costs and externalities rather than favouring or penalising electricity technologies merely according to their technological category; 
  • where public financial support or procurement is necessary, authorities should define the outcome or service required and allow competing technologies to determine how it can be delivered most efficiently, using transparent, proportionate, time-limited and competitive mechanisms wherever possible; 
  • competitive neutrality requires publicly and privately owned electricity companies to compete under equivalent market, regulatory and State aid conditions, while consumers should be able to participate actively through dynamic prices, flexibility, aggregators and competing contractual models; 
  • deeper European integration should reduce unnecessary national fragmentation while preserving proportionate regulation and allowing scientific evidence, technological progress and changing economic conditions to alter Europe’s electricity choices over time. 

LYMEC calls for: 

I. Technology-neutral climate neutrality 

  • European climate and electricity policy to pursue rapid and sustained reductions in greenhouse gas emissions without prescribing that climate neutrality must be achieved through a 100% renewable, nuclear-free or otherwise predetermined technological pathway; 
  • EU Member States to remain free to determine their own low-carbon electricity mix, including whether to use nuclear energy, while complying with common European climate, environmental, competition and safety standards; 
  • the rapid deployment of low-carbon generation and supporting infrastructure, including renewable generation, grids, storage and flexibility, while allowing nuclear energy to remain part of the long-term electricity mix in countries that choose to use it; 
  • EU Member States choosing to use nuclear energy to be free, subject to independent safety assessment and national policy choices, to construct new capacity, extend the operation of existing reactors and assess the technically and economically viable recommissioning of recently closed capacity; provided that such decisions are based on transparent lifecycle cost assessments, credible and fully financed plans for decommissioning and radioactive-waste management, adequate operator liability for nuclear accidents, and the internalisation of relevant environmental and safety risks.
  • regulatory, investment, sustainable-finance and State aid frameworks for low-carbon electricity to apply transparent and scientifically grounded criteria to technologies providing comparable climate and system benefits, while public procurement should specify measurable outcomes such as emissions intensity, reliability and system services rather than prescribe the technology used to deliver them; 
  • Member States to facilitate the repowering and expansion of existing low-carbon generation sites where existing grid connections, infrastructure and land use make this more efficient than comparable greenfield development, subject to the same substantive environmental and safety requirements; 
  • strong European research and innovation across renewable generation, storage, advanced grids, advanced nuclear technologies, Small Modular Reactors and nuclear fusion, with public research funding focused particularly on fundamental research, demonstration, first-of-a-kind technologies and identified market failures while commercially mature technologies increasingly rely on private capital; 
  • the progressive replacement of unabated fossil-fuel electricity generation by low-carbon alternatives while avoiding unnecessary long-lived fossil generation assets and carbon lock-in.
  • the phase-out of fossil fuels across the economy (including in transport, heating, and industry) to be driven primarily by comprehensive carbon pricing and technology-neutral market mechanisms, with any justified public support being competitive, time-limited and focused on outcomes rather than the large-scale roll-out of a specific technology;

II. Competitive markets and honest price signals 

  • carbon pricing to remain a central market-based instrument for reducing greenhouse gas emissions, in line with existing LYMEC policy, while energy taxation and electricity levies should increasingly reflect measurable externalities and cease systematically disadvantaging low-carbon electricity relative to the direct use of fossil fuels;
  • the minimum excise rates on electricity under the Energy Taxation Directive to be reduced to zero;
  • the progressive phase-out of environmentally harmful fossil-fuel subsidies and permanent operating subsidies for commercially mature generation technologies, with any justified public support for generation, capacity, storage or flexibility being transparent, proportionate, time-limited and competitively allocated wherever different resources can provide the required service; 
  • support schemes to preserve electricity-market signals, including incentives to reduce output when prices are negative or additional generation would aggravate congestion rather than rewarding production irrespective of its system value; 
  • broad wholesale or retail price caps and permanent administrative price-setting to be avoided, with affordability concerns addressed through targeted and transparent support; any exceptional emergency intervention should be temporary, targeted and designed to minimise distortions to price signals, competition, investment and cross-border trade; 
  • capacity mechanisms to be used only where transparent assessment demonstrates a remaining resource-adequacy problem, to be regularly reassessed, and to procure the required service rather than a predetermined technology, allowing non-discriminatory participation by demand response, storage, eligible cross-border capacity and firm low-carbon generation; 
  • deeper and more liquid European forward markets and fewer unnecessary barriers to bilateral and cross-border Power Purchase Agreements, alongside a broad choice of fixed-price, dynamic-price and long-term contracts so consumers and businesses can voluntarily choose how to allocate electricity-price risk; 
  • consumers, storage operators and other distributed resources to have non-discriminatory access to wholesale, balancing, congestion-management and ancillary-service markets, directly or through independent aggregators, with consumers free to monetise their flexibility without unnecessary dependence on their electricity supplier and without double counting; 
  • Member States to complete smart-meter deployment and ensure secure, standardised and user-controlled access to relevant consumption data for consumers and authorised service providers, enabling competition in dynamic tariffs, aggregation and other innovative electricity services; 
  • network tariffs to be transparent, non-discriminatory, technology-neutral and cost-reflective, allocating costs according to system use and cost causation while providing appropriate temporal and, where justified, locational signals for flexibility and congestion avoidance; 
  • electricity-market rules to permit competitive local flexibility and congestion-management markets where demand response, storage or generation can resolve constraints more efficiently than immediate network reinforcement; 
  • effective competitive neutrality between publicly and privately owned electricity companies, including equal access to markets and networks and consistent application of competition, procurement and State aid rules; 
  • stable and predictable frameworks for long-term electricity investment, avoiding retroactive changes to taxes, market rules or support schemes except where compelling public-interest considerations require them while preserving prospective democratic reform; 
  • assessments of competing technologies and public investment decisions to consider relevant full-system costs and benefits rather than relying solely on headline generation costs. 


III. A genuinely European and resilient electricity system 

  • the further completion of the European internal electricity market through sufficient cross-border interconnection, effective market coupling and the removal of unnecessary national regulatory barriers to electricity trade; 
  • European grid planning to reflect system-wide needs across the Union, including expected generation, demand, storage, electrification and cross-border flows, and to develop strategic high-capacity corridors, including HVDC infrastructure where justified by transparent system-needs and cost-benefit assessments; 
  • the costs of cross-border grid infrastructure to be allocated transparently according to measurable benefits and cost causation, preventing projects with substantial European benefits from being blocked because costs are concentrated in individual host or transit countries; 
  • transmission and distribution system operators to be able to undertake independently scrutinised anticipatory investments where credible scenarios demonstrate future capacity needs, while publishing sufficiently granular and regularly updated information on existing and planned connection capacity and network constraints; 
  • scarce grid-connection capacity to be allocated through transparent, non-discriminatory rules based on credible project readiness, objective milestones and the removal of inactive projects, while allowing voluntary flexible connection agreements that trade earlier access for clearly defined limitations on network use; 
  • permitting for generation, storage and grid infrastructure to become faster, fully digital and predictable through single points of contact, once-only data submission, transparent case tracking and clear deadlines, while authorities systematically remove duplicate or unnecessary procedures without weakening substantive environmental protection, public participation, property rights or safety standards; 
  • closer cooperation among European nuclear-safety authorities on standardised reactor technologies, including joint early reviews, reuse of technical assessments and common industrial and technical standards for Small and Advanced Modular Reactors where appropriate, while preserving the independence and final responsibility of competent national safety regulators; 
  • Europe to diversify strategic nuclear supply chains—including uranium sourcing, conversion, enrichment, fuel fabrication, critical components and specialised services—and maintain the scientific, engineering, industrial and regulatory expertise required to safely operate, assess, decommission and develop nuclear technologies; 
  • greater European cooperation on radioactive-waste management, including a framework for voluntary multinational geological repositories where these provide safer or more efficient solutions, subject to independent regulation, the polluter-pays principle, informed consent of the host state and affected communities, and continued financial responsibility of the state or operator generating the waste.
  • Strengthened European cooperation to protect critical electricity infrastructure, including offshore installations, interconnectors, substations and digitally connected energy systems, against physical sabotage, cyberattacks and hybrid threats, through coordinated risk assessments, joint resilience exercises, secure supply chains and cross-border emergency response mechanisms;

 

Archiving clause 

This resolution archives Resolution 6.02 “Reducing the Use of Fossil Fuels”, adopted at the LYMEC Congress in Amsterdam, the Netherlands, 8–10 April 2005; Resolution 6.03 “The future is Nuclear”, adopted at the LYMEC Congress in Utrecht, the Netherlands, 6–8 May 2011; and Resolution 6.05 “EmPOWERing Europe – The Single European Energy Market of the future”, adopted at the LYMEC Congress in Berlin, Germany, 23–25 October 2014.

Title: 3. Deregulate to Liberate: Making Life Affordable Again in Europe
Text:
Co-Signed by: Svensk Ungdom (SU), Centerpartiets Ungdomsförbund (CUF), Joventut Nacionalista de Catalunya, Jeunes Radicaux, LDLU, Momentum TizenX , LHG, Jungfreisinnige Schweiz

Noting that:

  • Rising energy costs and limited renewable energy production are increasing the cost of living and therefore place a financial burden on households.
  • Transportation and housing costs are increasing, with limited affordable and sustainable options available to citizens.
  • High taxes on food, restrictive policies in agriculture, and market barriers impact food affordability and access to innovative products.
  • Homelessness remains a pressing issue in Europe.
  • Rural areas suffer from limited infrastructure and connectivity, reducing their attractiveness.
  • Current recycling practices and waste management lack efficiency and sustainability.
  • Labour mobility and fair competition are hindered by regulatory and tax barriers across the EU.


Believing that:

  • Private investments in renewable energy, housing, and sustainable infrastructure are essential to reduce costs and ensure a high standard of living.
  • Supporting affordable transportation and standardized housing policies can help alleviate costs and promote fair access across Europe.
  • Enhancing recycling, food policy, and flexible labour conditions can create a resilient and sustainable economic environment.
  • Reducing bureaucratic hurdles and market barriers will facilitate access to affordable goods, services, and housing while promoting innovation.


LYMEC calls for:

Affordable and Sustainable Housing Solutions

  • Adopting the Housing First approach as seen in Finland to address homelessness, alongside year-round emergency programs and digitized official processes.
  • Supporting modular construction with standardized permits to accelerate building processes and reduce costs.
  • Implementing a rent-to-own model for newly built housing on public land
  • Rejecting rent caps and providing incentives, such as a real estate transfer tax allowance for first-time owner-occupied properties set relative to regional property prices.
  • Encouraging modular and flexible-use buildings that can adapt over time (e.g., from kindergarten to school or health center) to reduce long-term infrastructure costs.
  • Encouraging Member States and local authorities to liberalise restrictive zoning and planning regulations, facilitate higher-density and mixed-use developments, and allow the conversion and subdivision of existing buildings into housing, particularly in areas well connected to public transport.

Secure and Market-Based Energy System

  • Establishing a European Energy Union, and ensuring transnational grid stability.  
  • Introducing regional electricity price zones so consumers benefit directly from locally produced cheap renewable energy
  • Enabling citizen participation in local renewable energy projects 
  • Abolishing electricity taxes and energy-related levies at EU level and reduce VAT on electricity.
  • Strengthening and expanding the European Emissions Trading System (ETS) as the central market-based instrument for decarbonisation.
  • Returning a fixed, equal per-household climate dividend from European Emissions Trading System (ETS) revenues to directly reduce household energy costs and ensure that decarbonisation remains socially fair.

Affordable and Accessible Transportation

  • Supporting member states in introducing flat-rate public transport tickets to encourage public transit over personal vehicles.
  • Enhancing cross-border railway infrastructure and establishing an EU-wide high-speed rail network
  • Expanding the validity of national and regional flat-rate public transport tickets to regional services within cross-border regions, on a reciprocal basis between neighbouring states, and providing open timetable and fare data so that cross-border journeys can be planned and booked in one place.
  • Enabling the deployment of autonomous on-demand public transport services by establishing a harmonised EU regulatory framework for self-driving vehicles and supporting pilot programmes in rural and underserved areas.

Rural Development and Connectivity

  • Expanding 5G and broadband infrastructure in rural areas to improve internet access, creating a foundation for economic development and connectivity.  
  • Strengthening competition in mobile telecommunications by ensuring fair wholesale access for mobile virtual network operators (MVNOs) across all member states, enabling new market entrants to offer innovative services at competitive prices.
  • Park-and-ride facilities should be built at the edges of metropolitan regions and cities, combining affordable parking with convenient access points to local public transport services such as metro lines, and bus networks. 

Improved Waste Management and Recycling Standards 

  • Harmonizing the European deposit system and investing in materials research to improve recyclability and reusability of products.  
  • Strengthening global plastic agreements, and improving penalties for illegal waste disposal in oceans.  
  • Removing legal barriers for using recycled materials in housing construction, such as recycled concrete, linking waste reduction with sustainable building practices.

Enhanced Food and Agriculture Policies

  • Simplifying regulatory approval for GMOs and promoting agriculture based on consumer safety, lowering food production costs.
  • Streamlining regulatory approval for cultivated in-vitro meat and promoting its market access based on consumer safety, expanding food choice and lowering long-term production costs.  
  • Reducing regulatory barriers for agricultural trade to promote lower food prices through competition and open markets.
  • Cutting VAT on essential food items to lower food costs directly.  
  • Removing market barriers for plant-based alternatives by rejecting naming restrictions on terms like "burger" or "sausage", ending VAT discrimination against plant-based dairy substitutes, and ensuring technology-neutral food regulations that let consumers choose freely.

Flexible and Open Labour Market

  • Promoting flexible working conditions, enabling work and study mobility across Europe.  
  • Removing regulatory barriers, including the EU Minimum Wage Directive and the EU Working Time Directive, to increase cross-border labour flexibility.  
  • Reducing tax burdens and bureaucratic obstacles, increasing net income for individuals.
  • Enabling remote work across borders through digital infrastructure and harmonised rules, allowing young people to access higher-paying jobs without relocating to expensive cities.
  • Promoting gradual and flexible retirement models while strengthening financially sustainable, pre-funded pension systems and reducing reliance on systems where younger generations finance current pensions.
  • Promoting flexible childcare models, including registered childminders and employer-supported arrangements, by establishing EU-wide quality standards that focus on outcomes rather than prescriptive staff ratios.

Title: 5. Let the Market Split the Atom: A Technology-Neutral Framework for Nuclear Energy and a Competitive European Electricity Market
Text:
Co-signed by: Jongliberalen, Venstres Ungdom, Radikal Ungdom, Joventut Nacionalista

de Catalunya, Attistibai Youth, JOVD, LDLU, LHG, Jungfreisinnige Schweiz

de Catalunya, Attistibai Youth, JOVD, LDLU, LHG, ERPY

de Catalunya, Attistibai Youth, JOVD, LDLU, LHG, Jeunes MR

This motion replaces: 6.03 The future is Nuclear

Considering that:

  • Electricity demand in Europe will rise significantly as transport, heating and industry are electrified, and a competitive economy depends on affordable electricity that is available at every hour of the year;
  • Nuclear energy generates almost a quarter of the electricity produced in the European Union with very low lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions;
  • Several Member States that decided to phase out nuclear energy are now reversing or reconsidering these decisions, while early reactor closures have in some cases prolonged the use of fossil fuels for electricity generation;
  • Nineteen reactors of Soviet design in five Member States were built to run on Russian fuel, alternative supply for these reactors is still being established, and the European Union continues to import nuclear fuel and enrichment services from the Russian Federation;
  • Only a few Member States have made concrete progress towards deep geological repositories for spent nuclear fuel, and the rules on operator liability for nuclear damage and on the financing of decommissioning differ widely between Member States;
  • Under the Treaty establishing the European Atomic Energy Community, the European Parliament is in most cases only consulted, which leaves central decisions on nuclear safety, research and supply without democratic co-decision;
  • The United Kingdom and the United States have decided to regulate fusion energy outside their licensing regimes for nuclear fission, recognising its fundamentally different risk profile.

Noting that:

  • The Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union guarantees each Member State the right to determine the structure of its energy supply;
  • Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/1214 recognises nuclear energy as sustainable under conditions and Regulation (EU) 2024/1747 opens two-sided contracts for difference to it, while the InvestEU Programme still excludes nuclear power plants from support;
  • Large bidding zones and uniform network charges do not reflect physical grid bottlenecks, which leads to costly redispatch, curtailment of renewable generation and higher total system costs for consumers;
  • The European Commission has launched the European Industrial Alliance on Small Modular Reactors and presented a strategy to deploy small modular reactors in Europe by the early 2030s.

Believing that:

  • Climate protection is achieved most efficiently through a strong European Union Emissions Trading System that sets one price on carbon, while governments neither ban nor subsidise specific technologies, leaving the choice, including the role of nuclear energy, to consumers, investors and innovators on the basis of real costs and prices; 
  • Nuclear safety is not negotiable and must be guaranteed by independent regulators on the basis of science, not by political deadlines;
  • Energy supply that depends on autocratic regimes is a security risk and finances aggression against Europe;
  • Fusion energy can provide clean and abundant energy, and Europe should lead its development instead of regulating it away to other continents.

LYMEC calls for:

1. A competitive and technology-neutral electricity market

  • The retention of the merit order principle as the basis of European wholesale electricity markets;
  • Electricity prices that reflect the real costs of generation, transmission and load at each place and time, through a reconfiguration of bidding zones along physical grid constraints and, in the long term, locational pricing;
  • A reform of network charges towards time-variable and location-based tariffs, so that regions with high generation benefit from lower prices and total system costs fall for all users;
  • The consistent phase-out of state subsidies for all mature generation technologies, including fixed feed-in tariffs, and no new long-term revenue guarantees such as two-sided contracts for difference for any generation technology;
  • The removal of remaining regulatory barriers for energy storage, in particular the double charging of network fees and levies on stored electricity, and faster grid connection for projects that combine generation and storage;
  • Faster grid expansion through simplified and shorter permitting procedures and the most cost-efficient construction of new power lines;
  • A significantly faster rollout of smart metering systems and dynamic electricity tariffs, enabling digital grid management and the coupling of the electricity, heating and mobility sectors;
  • The European Investment Bank and all European Union funding instruments, including the InvestEU Programme, to treat all low-carbon technologies equally, neither privileging nor excluding nuclear energy.

2. The full-cost principle for nuclear energy

  • Operators of nuclear power plants to bear the cost of their activity, including decommissioning, waste disposal and liability for nuclear damage;
  • Mandatory decommissioning and waste disposal funds for all operators, separated from company assets, supervised by independent authorities and sized to cover the expected costs;
  • Harmonised European rules obliging operators to cover their liability for nuclear damage through insurance, financial security or pooled operator schemes, with minimum coverage based on realistic accident costs;
  • Member States to permit the construction of new nuclear power plants wherever operators bear these costs.

3. Ending political bans and modernising nuclear law

  • Member States to repeal legal bans on building, operating, extending and researching nuclear technologies, to modernise their nuclear legislation, and to grant independent regulators the sole authority to determine whether a nuclear installation is safe to operate, without limiting the right of operators to close a plant for economic reasons or the right of Member States to determine their energy mix through democratic decisions;
  • Reactors that fail to meet the requirements of Council Directive 2009/71/Euratom establishing a Community framework for the nuclear safety of nuclear installations, as verified by independent European peer review, to be shut down;
  • Member States to allow the conversion of shut-down reactors into research facilities.

4. A European framework for licensing, innovation and safety

  • The harmonisation of national rules for the operation, lifetime and construction of nuclear installations within the single European energy market;
  • The mutual recognition of reactor design approvals between national nuclear regulators, so that a design approved in one Member State does not require a complete new assessment in another;
  • Cross-border regulatory sandboxes for small modular reactors and fourth-generation designs such as molten salt reactors, fast breeder reactors and travelling wave reactors;
  • The freedom of companies to invest in the research, development and deployment of these technologies in every Member State;
  • The regular revision of risk assessments for all nuclear installations against natural disasters, terrorist attacks, cyber attacks and drone incursions, and the protection of nuclear installations as critical infrastructure.

5. Fuel sovereignty

  • A ban on new contracts with entities from the Russian Federation for uranium, conversion, enrichment and nuclear fuel, and a legally binding phase-out of existing supplies by 2030 at the latest;
  • The inclusion of Rosatom and its subsidiaries in European Union sanctions;
  • The accelerated licensing of alternative fuel for reactors of Soviet design and the expansion of conversion and enrichment capacity by European and allied suppliers.

6. Solving the waste question through research and European cooperation

  • Increased research funding for technologies that reduce the volume, radiotoxicity and lifetime of radioactive waste, in particular reprocessing and transmutation, including through the Euratom Research and Training Programme;
  • Member States to lift national bans on the reprocessing of spent fuel, under strict Euratom and International Atomic Energy Agency safeguards that prevent any military use of the resulting plutonium;
  • Deep geological repositories to be designed so that waste remains retrievable for future recycling technologies;
  • The establishment of a European expert body to identify geologically suitable sites for shared multinational repositories in Member States willing to host them;
  • A financing model for shared repositories in which host countries are compensated, operators pay for the waste they produce and Member States cover legacy waste in proportion to their share of nuclear generation.

7. Fusion energy

  • A European legal framework for fusion energy outside the law on nuclear fission, proportionate to its risk profile and open to innovation;
  • The European Union to become the global frontrunner in fusion energy by supporting basic research, demonstration plants and lighthouse projects, including ITER and its successor DEMO, as well as public-private partnerships with fusion start-ups;
  • Research budgets for fusion and other breakthrough energy technologies that accept failures as a normal part of research.

8. Democratic control over European nuclear policy

  • A reform of the Treaty establishing the European Atomic Energy Community that grants the European Parliament full co-decision rights on all nuclear legislation.

9. International research and material partnerships

  • Deepened cooperation with trusted democratic partners on nuclear research, reactor design, and the safe handling of nuclear materials, building on existing frameworks such as Euratom cooperation agreements;
  • Joint investment with these partners in diversifying the supply of uranium, conversion, and enrichment services away from dependence on the Russian Federation, including support for mining and enrichment capacity in allied and partner countries;
  • Coordinated export-control and non-proliferation standards among these partners, ensuring that expanded research and material cooperation strengthens the international non-proliferation regime rather than weakening it.

Title: 2. Making Europe a Global Leader in Pharmaceutical Innovation
Text:
Submitted by: Jeunes MR

Co-signed: Joventut Nacionalista de Catalunya, NEON, VU, ZeMolodizhka, PSG Mladi, Alliance Youth, Jongliberalen, JUNOS, Radikal Ungdom, Young Croatian Liberals, Jonge Democraten, YDM Vesna, Gibanje Svoboda Mladi, Momentum TizenX, Youth Forum of Naša stranka (Bosnia and Herzegovina), JOVD, LHG, Centerpartiets Ungdomsförbund(CUF), Lithuanian Liberal Youth, Jungfreisinnige Schweiz

Considering that:

  • a competitive European pharmaceutical sector is essential to public health, scientific progress, skilled employment and Europe’s ability to respond to health crises;
  • In 2022, the European pharmaceutical industry contributed €311 billion to the EU’s gross value added and generated approximately 2.3 million direct and indirect jobs ;
  • Each employee in the pharmaceutical sector generates on average €225,300 in value added, according to PwC ;
  • In 2024, EU pharmaceutical exports to third countries totalled €313.4 billion, underscoring the global competitiveness of the sector ;
  • The COVID-19 crisis demonstrated that a strong pharmaceutical sector is essential for the EU’s strategic autonomy and sovereignty ; 
  • European companies, including BioNTech, played a pioneering role in developing and producing mRNA vaccines — with industrial production largely taking place within the EU (Germany, Belgium, France, the Netherlands) ; 
  • Over 70 % of vaccines produced in the EU were exported to more than 160 countries, making the Union a global production hub ; 
  • EU public funds directly supported research, development, and industrial scale-up during the pandemic ; 
  • Pharmaceutical leadership requires an environment in which research can develop into viable businesses, innovative treatments and reliable manufacturing capacity;
  • concentrated supply chains and dependence on a limited number of suppliers can expose patients and healthcare systems to shortages and external disruption;
  • international trade and scientific cooperation support pharmaceutical innovation, while diversified partnerships strengthen Europe’s resilience;
  • gaps in understanding women’s health and sex-related differences in treatment responses represent both unmet medical needs and an important frontier for European research and innovation;
  • industrial success must translate into measurable improvements in the availability, safety, effectiveness and affordability of medicines;

Noting that:

  • the EU’s framework for clinical trials and the Clinical Trials Information System provide a basis for multinational research and transparent reporting;
  • European initiatives concerning critical medicines address the relationship between manufacturing capacity, diversified supply chains and security of supply;
  • differences in the absorption, distribution, metabolism and elimination of medicines can affect treatment responses, making appropriate investigation of sex-related differences relevant to pharmaceutical development and safety;
  • women’s health extends beyond reproductive health and requires attention across therapeutic fields and throughout life;
  • universities, hospitals, pharmaceutical companies and biotechnology SMEs have complementary roles in translating scientific discoveries into treatments;

Believing that:

  • Europe should aspire to global pharmaceutical leadership through scientific excellence, entrepreneurship, open competition and predictable regulation;
  • strengthening European capabilities should go together with international cooperation and diversified trade;
  • addressing unmet needs in women’s health should be a strategic research and investment priority, with clear objectives and accountable funding;
  • scientific inclusion requires research populations and analyses appropriate to the condition and intended treatment population, with therapeutic decisions grounded in evidence;
  • public support should address identified needs, attract additional investment and deliver demonstrable public value;
  • innovation, patient safety and access to treatment are mutually reinforcing objectives;

LYMEC calls for:

1. Strengthening European pharmaceutical competitiveness and commercial leadership by:

  • calling on EU institutions and Member States, within their respective competences, to provide predictable regulatory and investment conditions for pharmaceutical research, development and manufacturing;
  • simplifying duplicative administrative procedures and improving coordination between authorities while preserving scientific, ethical and safety standards;
  • facilitating access to competitive research funding, growth capital and regulatory advice for European startups, SMEs and biotechnology companies;
  • supporting partnerships between universities, hospitals and businesses to bring discoveries through clinical development and into production;
  • maintaining effective intellectual property protection alongside competition and timely entry of generic and biosimilar medicines in accordance with applicable rules;
  • pursuing trade agreements and regulatory cooperation that reduce unnecessary barriers, diversify export markets and preserve European health standards;
  • The European Commission to seek the elimination or substantial reduction of tariffs and non-tariff barriers for European pharmaceutical products exported to important markets.

2. Building resilient European manufacturing and medicine supplies by:

  • identifying critical medicines, active ingredients and production stages exposed to significant supply vulnerabilities;
  • directing transparent, proportionate and regularly reviewed support towards these vulnerabilities, combining European investment with diversified international sourcing;
  • strengthening coordinated shortage monitoring, early notification and contingency planning between competent authorities, manufacturers and distributors;
  • developing risk-based stock arrangements that consider shelf life, patient needs and cross-border solidarity;
  • incorporating quality, supply reliability and continuity into public procurement, including multiple suppliers where appropriate;
  • ensuring that resilience measures remain compatible with competition and avoid creating new dependencies on individual companies or suppliers;

3. Making women’s health a strategic pillar of pharmaceutical innovation by:

  • establishing a clearly identified women’s health research and innovation priority within existing European funding programmes, with dedicated competitive calls, transparent budgets and measurable objectives;
  • supporting research into conditions specific to women, disproportionately affecting them or presenting differently in women, including endometriosis, polycystic ovary syndrome and sex-related differences in cardiovascular disease and treatment responses;
  • strengthening the translation of this research into validated diagnostics, medicines and treatment strategies through partnerships between researchers, clinicians, patients and businesses;
  • facilitating access to finance and scientific advice for companies developing solutions to unmet needs in women’s health, subject to the same standards of clinical evidence and safety as other innovations;
  • requiring publicly funded clinical trials to justify recruitment against the intended treatment population, explain exclusions and prespecify sex-related analyses where scientifically relevant, with adequate statistical planning;
  • supporting research methods that appropriately account for age, hormonal status and other relevant biological factors, while avoiding unjustified blanket exclusions;
  • strengthening the analysis of medicine effectiveness and adverse reactions by sex, and requiring reassessment of dosage, product information or clinical recommendations when sufficiently robust evidence warrants it;
  • publishing progress on research funding, trial participation, evidence gaps and resulting therapeutic advances, while protecting personal data and research participants;

4. Turning pharmaceutical leadership into better access and accountable results by:

  • improving coordination between regulatory assessment, health technology assessment and national access and reimbursement processes, while respecting their distinct responsibilities;
  • promoting transparent decisions based on clinical benefit, unmet medical needs and the sustainability of healthcare systems;
  • Encouraging Member States to jointly negotiate the prices of expensive medicines with pharmaceutical companies, while promoting greater transparency regarding research, development and production costs, to strengthen their bargaining power and ensure affordable access to innovative treatments across Europe;
  • supporting professional training in pharmaceutical research, manufacturing, regulatory science and the assessment of sex-related differences;
  • enabling secure and scientifically validated uses of health data and digital tools, with effective privacy and cybersecurity safeguards;
  • calling on the European Commission, together with Member States, to publish within twelve months of taking up these recommendations a costed implementation roadmap identifying responsible authorities, funding sources and milestones;
  • assessing progress annually across investment, manufacturing resilience, shortages, SME growth, women’s health research and patient access, with an independent review after three years;
